entry.title: When Code Is Cheap, Design the Promises
entry.summary: AI has made code cheap to write but no cheaper to trust. That changes what a specification is for, and it makes tracking how a program's promises change over time a core part of software engineering.
entry.content:
Generating code is no longer the expensive part of building software. Describe a routine to a model and you get an apparently correct implementation in seconds. Ask for a change and it’s done just as fast. What hasn’t become cheaper is knowing whether the code does what it should, and whether it still does after the tenth change made by something that need not remember the first two.

The essay on why Nex is designed for correctness argues that contracts are the verification layer generated code most lacks. This post follows that argument in two directions. The first is what happens to specification and documentation when the implementation becomes the cheap part. The second is why tracking how software evolves becomes more important, and a practical way to do it.

The specification becomes the source

Here is a specification of the kind that gets written in tickets, design docs and prompts every day:

Wrap the text so that no line is longer than the given width.

A person reading this fills in the gaps from experience. A model fills them in too, with whatever is most plausible. And believe me, there are plenty of gaps. What happens to a word longer than the width: is it split, left sticking out past the edge, or rejected? Are runs of spaces kept? How full should each line be? An implementation that puts every word on a line of its own obeys the sentence exactly, but as you can imagine, no one will accept it.

Now the same specification as a contract. It is written as a deferred (or abstract) class, which states what wrap must do and says nothing about how:

deferred class Wrapper
feature
  wrap(text: String, width: Integer): Array[String]
    note "Break `text` into lines of at most `width` characters."
  require
    positive_width: width > 0
    words_fit: words(text).all(fn (w) => w.length <= width)
  deferred
  ensure
    lines_fit: result.all(fn (line) => line.length <= width)
    same_words: " ".join(result) = " ".join(words(text))
    filled: is_filled(result, width)
  end

  words(text: String): Array[String]
    note "The words of `text`, without the spaces around them."
  do
    result := text.split(" ").filter(fn (w) => w.length > 0)
  end

  is_filled(lines: Array[String], width: Integer): Boolean
    note "No line has room for the first word of the line after it."
  do
    result := true
    from let i := 0 until result = false or i >= lines.length - 1 do
      let next_word := words(lines.get(i + 1)).get(0)
      if lines.get(i).length + 1 + next_word.length <= width then
        result := false
      end
      i := i + 1
    end
  end
end

Each clause answers one of the questions the prose left open:

  • words_fit makes a word longer than the line the caller’s problem. The wrapper never has to split or hyphenate anything.
  • same_words says the lines hold exactly the words of the text, in order, with single spaces between them. Nothing is lost, added or reordered, and runs of spaces aren’t kept.
  • lines_fit is the width rule from the prose.
  • filled rules out the one-word-per-line answer: no line may have room left for the first word of the line after it.

words and is_filled have bodies, but they aren’t the implementation. They are the vocabulary the contract is written in, and they are small enough to check by reading them.

Together, the clauses pin down the output. For a given width and any text with at least one word, exactly one list of lines satisfies them all. (For an empty text, both [] and [""] pass, a gap small enough to leave open.) What the clauses don’t pin down is how to compute the answer.

What’s left for the model

The algorithm is what’s left. A model writes it in a class that inherits the specification:

class Greedy_Wrapper
  inherit Wrapper
feature
  wrap(text: String, width: Integer): Array[String] do
    result := []
    let line := ""
    across words(text) as w do
      if line.length = 0 then
        line := w
      elseif line.length + 1 + w.length <= width then
        line := line + " " + w
      else
        result.add(line)
        line := w
      end
    end
    if line.length > 0 then
      result.add(line)
    end
  end
end

The class doesn’t repeat a single clause. Nex attaches the inherited contract to the redefined wrap, so every call is checked against Wrapper:

let w: Wrapper := create Greedy_Wrapper
print(w.wrap("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog", 10))
-- ["the quick", "brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy", "dog"]
print(w.wrap("  lots   of   space  ", 10))
-- ["lots of", "space"]

The algorithm is short, but it is easy to get slightly wrong. Here is the same loop with the space between two words left out of the length check:

      elseif line.length + w.length <= width then   -- forgot the space

Nothing about this version looks wrong, and it wraps the sentence above correctly. But when two words plus their space come to one more than the width, it puts them on one line anyway. "hello world" is 11 characters, so w.wrap("hello world", 10) fails:

Error: Postcondition violation: lines_fit

The one-word-per-line implementation is even shorter:

  wrap(text: String, width: Integer): Array[String] do
    result := words(text)
  end

It fails with Postcondition violation: filled. Without the filled clause, though, it would pass. Every line fits, and every word is there in order. The prose never said lines should be full, so the contract has to say it, or the model is free not to. A contract decides which gaps matter, and anything it leaves open is the implementer’s choice. Leaving something open should be a decision too.

filled is itself a decision. It asks for greedy filling, one line at a time. A wrapper that balances line lengths, the way typesetting systems do, leaves room on some lines on purpose, and it would break filled. If that is what you want, the promise has to change, not just the code.

This changes the role of the specification. When code was expensive, the specification was a step on the way to the code, and once the code existed it became the reference. When code is cheap, the relationship turns around. Greedy_Wrapper can be regenerated, rewritten by a different model, or replaced in an afternoon with a faster version. Wrapper is what stays. It is the target a generator aims at and the test that tells you whether it hit it.

For that to work, the specification has to be precise enough to check. Prose specifications were always ambiguous. The ambiguity used to be resolved by the person writing the code, who could ask what was meant. A model resolves it by guessing, and it often won’t say that it guessed.

Two kinds of documentation

If the contract states what the code does, what is left for documentation?

Much of what we have written in the past as documentation is restatement: a comment above wrap saying it wraps text, a Javadoc block listing the parameters, a wiki page describing the API. That kind of writing was useful when reading code was slow. A model can now produce it on demand, and in a Nex program most of it is already in the contract. nex doc extracts the contract view of a class, with signatures, notes and assertions and no implementation. Here is the entry for wrap:

### wrap(`text: String`, `width: Integer`): `Array[String]` *(deferred)*
🌐 Public
Break `text` into lines of at most `width` characters.

**Parameters:**
- `text`: `String`
- `width`: `Integer`

**Returns:** `Array[String]`

**Pre-conditions:**
- **positive_width**: `width > 0`
- **words_fit**: `words(text).all(fn (w) => w.length <= width)`

**Post-conditions:**
- **lines_fit**: `result.all(fn (line) => line.length <= width)`
- **same_words**: `" ".join(result) = " ".join(words(text))`
- **filled**: `is_filled(result, width)`

That view is generated from the code, so it can’t drift away from it. If it’s wrong, the code is wrong.

What the contract can’t hold is why. Why is a word longer than the line the caller’s problem, instead of something the wrapper hyphenates? Why fill lines greedily instead of balancing them? Which alternatives were tried and dropped, and what ruled them out? A model can’t regenerate those answers, because they aren’t in the code. They live in someone’s head, in a meeting that wasn’t written up, or in the requirements of whatever displays the text.

So documentation splits in two:

  1. What the code promises. It belongs in the code as contracts, where it is executed and checked. Writing it in prose elsewhere is a liability, because the prose will go out of date and nothing will notice.
  2. Why it promises that. It belongs in prose, because it can’t be checked. That also means it decays unless someone keeps it up on purpose.

The first kind gets easier with AI, since a model is good at drafting contracts for a human to review. The second kind gets more valuable. When anyone can produce an implementation, the reasoning behind the design is the part that is hard to replace.

Why tracking evolution matters more

A codebase is a history of changes, and keeping track of that history has always been hard. AI makes it harder in three ways.

Volume. A team that used to merge ten changes a day can now merge a hundred. Review capacity didn’t grow at the same rate. Reading every line of every diff with care was never fully realistic, and now it isn’t close.

Short or no memory. A developer who changed a routine last month remembers why. An agent starting a new session doesn’t. It sees the code as it is now, not the decisions that shaped it, so it can undo a deliberate choice that looks like an accident from the outside.

Agents fix the check instead of the code. When a change makes a test or an assertion fail, the quickest way to make the failure go away is to change the check. People do this too, but an agent told to “make the build pass” may do it without hesitation, and without saying so.

Here is what that looks like. Take a small account class whose contract has been in use for a while:

class Account
  note "A bank account that never goes overdrawn."
feature
  balance: Integer

  deposit(amount: Integer)
    note "Add `amount` to the balance."
  require
    positive: amount > 0
  do
    balance := balance + amount
  ensure
    increased: balance = old balance + amount
  end

  withdraw(amount: Integer)
    note "Take `amount` out of the account."
  require
    positive: amount > 0
    enough: amount <= balance
  do
    balance := balance - amount
  ensure
    decreased: balance = old balance - amount
  end

invariant
  never_overdrawn: balance >= 0
end

Someone asks for a flat fee of 1 on every withdrawal. The agent changes the body:

  withdraw(amount: Integer)
  require
    positive: amount > 0
    enough: amount <= balance
  do
    balance := balance - amount - 1   -- new: a flat fee
  ensure
    decreased: balance = old balance - amount
  end

The contract catches the change immediately:

Error: Postcondition violation: decreased

That’s what contracts are for: to catch routines that no longer keep their promises. The right response requires a decision. Either the promise changes, so callers learn that a withdrawal costs amount + 1, or the fee goes somewhere else. The quick response is to loosen the postcondition until it passes:

  ensure
    decreased: balance < old balance

The program runs again. Every check passes. And a promise callers depended on, that a withdrawal takes out exactly what was asked for, is gone. Any caller that computed the expected balance is now wrong, and nothing reports it.

In a diff of a few hundred lines, that one-line change is easy to miss. It is also the most important line in the change.

Each version is a subclass of the last one

Nex already has rules for changing a contract safely. They apply to inheritance. A redefinition in a subclass may weaken a precondition, because it must accept every call the parent accepted. It may strengthen a postcondition, because it must keep every promise the parent made. It is bound by every inherited invariant. Nex enforces this by combining contracts down the hierarchy: preconditions with or, postconditions and invariants with and. (The post on classes and their contracts works through this in detail.)

The reason for those rules is substitutability. A client written against the parent must still work when it receives a child object.

A new version of a module has the same problem in time instead of space. Every client written against version 1 should still work against version 2. So the same rules apply:

  • Version 2 may accept more than version 1 (a weaker or removed require clause).
  • Version 2 may promise more than version 1 (a new or stronger ensure or invariant clause).
  • Anything else, such as accepting less, promising less, or removing a public feature, is a breaking change and should be announced as one.

This is what semantic versioning is trying to capture, stated in terms that can be checked. “Is this change backwards compatible?” becomes “Is version 2 a valid subcontract of version 1?”

The word-wrap specification is already set up this way. Wrapper is the parent, and every implementation, generated or not, is a subclass bound by its contract. Between releases there is no such parent. Version 1 isn’t a class that version 2 inherits from, it’s just an older commit. Nex checks the rule automatically across inheritance. Nothing checks it between releases, so the job falls to the review process. The good news is that contracts make that job small, because the parts that need checking are exactly the contracts.

A practical workflow

The idea is to make the change to the contracts its own reviewable artifact, separate from the change to the code.

1. Keep the contract view in the repository. Generate it with nex doc and commit the output next to the code, for example under docs/contracts/. In CI, regenerate it and fail if it differs from what was committed:

$ nex doc src docs/contracts
$ git diff --exit-code docs/contracts

Any change that touches a contract now has to change a file in docs/contracts/, and that file shows up in the pull request on its own.

2. Read the contract diff first. Here is the agent’s “fix” from the previous section, as it appears in the contract view:

 **Post-conditions:**
-- **decreased**: `balance = old balance - amount`
+- **decreased**: `balance < old balance`

A postcondition got weaker, so this is a breaking change. It doesn’t matter how many lines of implementation came with it. Compare a change that adds a withdrawal counter:

 - **balance**: `Integer` 🌐 Public
+- **withdrawals**: `Integer` 🌐 Public
 ...
 **Post-conditions:**
 - **decreased**: `balance = old balance - amount`
+- **counted**: `withdrawals = old withdrawals + 1`

A new feature and a new promise, with nothing taken away: compatible. And a daily limit:

 **Pre-conditions:**
 - **positive**: `amount > 0`
 - **enough**: `amount <= balance`
+- **within_daily_limit**: `amount <= 500`

The precondition got stronger. A call that worked in version 1, withdraw(600) on a balance of 1000, now fails with Precondition violation: within_daily_limit. That’s breaking, even though the code change is a single line.

Reading the diff takes judgement. When a clause is edited instead of added or removed, someone has to decide whether the new one is weaker or stronger. But the diff shows where to look, and it is usually a few lines, however large the change to the code.

3. Diffs that change only the body are refactorings. If the contract view didn’t change, the change claims to keep every promise, and the contracts check that claim each time the code runs. Those changes still deserve review, but a different kind: tests, performance and readability, not “did the meaning change?”

4. Require a human to approve contract changes. On GitHub, a CODEOWNERS entry for docs/contracts/ makes approval from a named person mandatory for any change to that directory. An agent can propose a new promise. A person decides whether to make it.

5. Write down the why, close to the change. When a contract changes on purpose, record the reason in a short decision record: one file per decision, such as docs/decisions/0007-withdrawal-fee.md, saying what changed, why, and what was considered instead. When an agent made the change, include the request it was given. A year later, the contract diff tells you what changed, and the decision record tells you why. With both, a new team member or a new agent session can reconstruct how the module got to its current state.

None of this needs new tools. It needs contracts in the code, a generated view of them, and a rule that changes to that view are reviewed as changes in meaning.

Limits

Runtime contracts aren’t proofs. A contract catches a violation when the code path that breaks it runs. A path that no test or user exercises can still break a promise without anyone noticing. The contract view only tracks promises that were written down, so behaviour nobody specified can change without leaving a trace in docs/contracts/. That is one more reason to write the contract in the first place.

The why still depends on people. Nothing checks a decision record, and an unmaintained one is as misleading as a stale comment.

The history of the promises

For most of the history of software, writing the code was the hard part, and the specification was something we wrote to help us write it. That is no longer true. Code can be produced, thrown away and produced again. What a program promises, and how those promises changed and why, is the part that has to be kept.

In a language where promises are written in the code and checked, that history is something you can read and review.

entry.title: Classes and their Contracts
entry.summary: How Nex allows the specification of an abstract datatype to live in the code itself instead of a comment or document.
entry.content:
One of the first lessons taught in object-oriented programming courses is that classes are an expression of an abstract datatype. An abstract datatype has a public API (an interface) and is supposed to keep its invariants. An invariant is a statement that is always true about an object of the class, as seen from the client’s perspective. For example, if a class represents the abstract notion of a push-down stack, then the implementation must assure the client that after a successful call to the pop method, the size of the stack will not go negative.

In this post, let’s look at the implementation of another abstract datatype – a text buffer with a cursor, the kind of thing behind any text field or editor. It exposes the following methods in its API:

  1. insert(text) – insert text at the current cursor position. text must be non-null and non-empty.
  2. delete_back(n) – delete n characters before the cursor (like Backspace). 0 < n <= cursor.
  3. length – return the number of characters in the buffer.
  4. cursor – return the cursor position (positions start at 0).

The implementation must also maintain the class invariant 0 <= cursor and cursor <= length.

A Java implementation of the above specification follows:

/**
 * A text buffer with an insertion cursor.
 * Invariant: 0 <= cursor <= length()
 */
public class TextBuffer {
    protected final StringBuilder content = new StringBuilder();
    protected int cursor = 0;

    public int length() { return content.length(); }
    public int cursor() { return cursor; }

    /**
     * Inserts s at the cursor and moves the cursor past it.
     * @param s must be non-null and non-empty
     * Postcondition: length grows by s.length(); cursor advances by s.length()
     */
    public void insert(String s) {
        if (s == null || s.isEmpty())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("s must be non-empty");
        int oldLength = length(), oldCursor = cursor;   // manual "old"
        content.insert(cursor, s);
        cursor += s.length();
        assert length() == oldLength + s.length();
        assert cursor == oldCursor + s.length();
        assert 0 <= cursor && cursor <= length();      // invariant, by hand
    }

    /**
     * Deletes n characters before the cursor, like Backspace.
     * @param n must satisfy 0 < n <= cursor
     */
    public void deleteBack(int n) {
        if (n <= 0 || n > cursor)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("need 0 < n <= cursor");
        int oldLength = length(), oldCursor = cursor;
        content.delete(cursor - n, cursor);
        cursor -= n;
        assert length() == oldLength - n;
        assert cursor == oldCursor - n;
        assert 0 <= cursor && cursor <= length();
    }
}

The above implementation is as close to the specification as it can be, but most of the contract lives in comments. Though documenting the public API of a class like this in Javadoc (or its equivalent in other languages) is considered great software engineering practice, its value is minimal because no tool can reliably check and enforce prose. For instance, if someone changes deleteBack to clamp n instead of rejecting it and forgets the comment, nothing complains.

Having said that, the programmer has not completely ignored the API’s contracts. As you can see, insert makes sure the content length and cursor are incremented correctly once the method finishes its job. Though this is good practice, every postcondition that mentions the previous state needs locals captured at the start. This is a tedious job and in practice people skip it. As a result, postconditions mostly go unwritten.

What about the class invariant? Though it is part of almost all high-level design documents, the class invariant is not a language concept in Java (and most other industrial languages). As a consequence, invariant checks have to be repeated at the end of every public method in the form of an assert. Add moveCursorTo(int) next month and whoever writes it will almost certainly forget the check.

Another catch for Java programmers is that assert is off by default. Assertions run only with the -ea flag.

The bottom line is that specification and defensive code get mixed up, and any comment that keeps track of the original design assumptions soon goes out of sync with the code.

Before critiquing the Java version further, let’s see how the same class looks in Nex, where preconditions, postconditions and invariants are first-class language constructs.

class Text_Buffer
feature -- Access

  length: Integer
  do
    result := content.length
  end

  cursor: Integer

feature -- Editing
  insert(s: String)
    note "Insert `s` at the cursor and move the cursor past it."
  require
    not_empty: s.length > 0
  do
    let prefix := content.substring(0, cursor)
    content := prefix + s + content.substring(cursor, content.length)
    cursor := cursor + s.length
  ensure
    grown: length = old length + s.length
    cursor_advanced: cursor = old cursor + s.length
  end

  delete_back(n: Integer)
    note "Delete `n` characters before the cursor, like Backspace."
  require
    positive: n > 0
    enough_text_before_cursor: n <= cursor
  do
    let prefix := content.substring(0, cursor - n)
    let suffix := content.substring(cursor, content.length)
    content := prefix + suffix
    cursor := cursor - n
  ensure
    shrunk: length = old length - n
    cursor_moved_back: cursor = old cursor - n
  end

  set_cursor(n: Integer)
  require
    cursor_in_range: n >= 0 and n <= length
  do
    cursor := n
  end

feature -- Implementation
  content: String

invariant
    cursor_in_range: 0 <= cursor and cursor <= length
end

-- Tests
let buf := create Text_Buffer
buf.insert("hello")
buf.insert("world")
assert buf.content = "helloworld"
buf.set_cursor(5)
buf.insert(", ")
assert buf.content = "hello, world"
buf.set_cursor(3)
buf.delete_back(2)
assert buf.content = "hlo, world"
buf.insert("el")
assert buf.content = "hello, world"

In the Nex definition of Text_Buffer, the contract sits next to the code it describes. Notice how the three kinds of assertion divide the work of completely enforcing the specification:

  1. require is the client’s obligation. Calling delete_back(5) with the cursor at position 2 is a bug in the caller.
  2. ensure is the supplier’s obligation. If insert leaves the cursor in the wrong place, the bug is in this routine. old refers to a value on entry, so the postcondition can relate the before and after states.
  3. invariant must hold whenever an object is observable from outside: after creation, and before and after every call from a client. Here it says the cursor can never run off either end of the text.

Tools like nex doc can extract the contract view of the class, which shows signatures, header comments and assertions with no implementation. That view is generated from the code, so it can’t drift away from it.

There’s no null check on s because Nex is null-safe: a String argument is always attached to a value, so the type system rules out null.

Preconditions vs. defensive programming

Let’s go back and look at the Java class again. There we see deleteBack throwing IllegalArgumentException. It turns “n must not exceed the cursor” from an obligation on the caller into defined behaviour of the method: delete too much and you get an exception, which callers may catch and rely on. Java’s own guidance reinforces this. Oracle’s “Programming With Assertions” guide says not to use assert for argument checking in public methods, and to throw exceptions instead.

Design by Contract takes the opposite view, which Bertrand Meyer calls the non-redundancy principle: the body of a well-designed routine should never test its own precondition. The caller is responsible for knowing where the cursor is. An editor that sends Backspace with nothing before the cursor has a bug in its key handling, and the buffer shouldn’t absorb it. The runtime check exists only to catch that bug during development and testing. Defensive programming, where every routine checks everything just in case, produces code that is longer and slower and leaves it unclear who is responsible for what.

Note one caveat here: external input is not covered by preconditions. A keystroke or a pasted clipboard string should be validated once, by the module that receives it, and from then on the program can rely on contracts.

Contracts and inheritance

Dynamic binding means a client written against Text_Buffer might actually be working with an object of its child class. The client can only reason with the contract it can see. So every redefinition has to be a subcontract that honours that contract:

  • The precondition may only weaken: the redefinition must accept at least everything the parent accepted.
  • The postcondition may only strengthen: it must deliver at least everything the parent promised.
  • The invariant is inherited, and descendants can only add to it.

There is no language-level support in Java or Python to enforce these rules. That means the programmer who is implementing a child class can end up breaking the contracts of the abstract datatype. Imagine someone implementing a buffer with a maximum length. In Java, it might look like this:

public class BoundedBuffer extends TextBuffer {
    private final int capacity;

    public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

    @Override
    public void insert(String s) {
        int room = capacity - length();
        if (room > 0)
            super.insert(s.substring(0, Math.min(room, s.length())));
    }
}

This compiles and runs without complaint. Now consider a client written against TextBuffer, for example an autocomplete feature:

void complete(TextBuffer buf, String suffix) {
    buf.insert(suffix);
    highlight(buf.cursor() - suffix.length(), buf.cursor());  // select what was inserted
}

With a BoundedBuffer that truncates, the highlight now covers text the user typed, not the completion. When the buffer is already full, it covers characters that were there before. No contract violation is reported. Even the parent’s asserts pass, because super.insert checks its postcondition against the truncated string it was handed, not the string the client asked to insert. The contract the client relied on is broken, and none of the checks can see it.

Now let’s look at the same child class implemented in Nex:

class Bounded_Buffer
inherit Text_Buffer

feature
  capacity: Integer

create
  make_with_capacity(n: Integer)
  do
    capacity := n
  end

feature
  insert(s: String)
  do
    let room := capacity - length
    if room > 0 then
      super.insert(s.substring(0, room.min(s.length)))
    end
  end
end

let b_buf: Text_Buffer := create Bounded_Buffer.make_with_capacity(10)
b_buf.insert("he")
b_buf.insert("llo, ")
assert b_buf.content = "hello, "
b_buf.insert("world") -- raise postcondition violation

Bounded_Buffer.insert contains no assertions, but it inherits grown: length = old length + s.length and cursor_advanced from Text_Buffer. Crucially, they are evaluated for the call the client actually made, with the client’s s. The first time a string is truncated, you get a postcondition violation that names Bounded_Buffer.insert as the culprit. super.insert checking its own contract on the shorter string doesn’t hide the problem.

Putting the limit in the parent’s contract

The real problem isn’t in Bounded_Buffer. It’s that Text_Buffer’s contract promises something a bounded buffer can’t deliver: any non-empty string can always be inserted. No redefinition of insert can fix that. When a string doesn’t fit, the only honest thing a bounded insert can do is refuse it, and refusing means a stronger precondition, which the subcontracting rules forbid.

The fix is to make the parent’s contract admit that a buffer may run out of room. Add a query, has_room, to Text_Buffer and make it part of insert’s precondition:

class Text_Buffer
feature -- Access
  -- length and cursor as before

  has_room(s: String): Boolean
    note "Can `s` be inserted without exceeding the buffer's limits?"
  do
    result := true
  end

feature -- Editing
  insert(s: String)
    note "Insert `s` at the cursor and move the cursor past it."
  require
    not_empty: s.length > 0
    room_available: has_room(s)
  do
    let prefix := content.substring(0, cursor)
    content := prefix + s + content.substring(cursor, content.length)
    cursor := cursor + s.length
  ensure
    grown: length = old length + s.length
    cursor_advanced: cursor = old cursor + s.length
  end

  -- delete_back, set_cursor, content and the invariant as before
end

A plain Text_Buffer always has room, so for its clients nothing changes in practice. But the contract now says, in code, that a client must establish has_room(s) before calling insert. A bounded buffer only has to say what “room” means for it:

class Bounded_Buffer
inherit Text_Buffer

feature
  capacity: Integer

  has_room(s: String): Boolean
  do
    result := length + s.length <= capacity
  end

create
  make_with_capacity(n: Integer)
  require
    non_negative: n >= 0
  do
    capacity := n
  end

invariant
  within_capacity: length <= capacity
end

Bounded_Buffer doesn’t redefine insert at all. It inherits the parent’s body, precondition and postconditions unchanged. Its only addition to the contract is the invariant within_capacity, which is AND-ed with the inherited cursor_in_range.

Clients written against Text_Buffer now ask before they insert:

let buf: Text_Buffer := create Bounded_Buffer.make_with_capacity(10)
buf.insert("he")
buf.insert("llo, ")
assert not buf.has_room("world")
if buf.has_room("wor") then
  buf.insert("wor")
end
assert buf.content = "hello, wor"
buf.insert("!") -- raise precondition violation

The last call fails with Precondition violation: room_available, and the error points at the call, not at insert. That’s the right verdict: the buffer was full, the client could have asked, and it didn’t. In the previous version the same mistake produced a postcondition violation that blamed Bounded_Buffer.insert, and in Java it produced nothing at all.

Isn’t this just a stronger precondition in disguise? For a given object, a Bounded_Buffer does accept fewer strings than an unbounded one. The difference is that clients were told. The precondition a client reads is has_room(s), the same expression in both classes, and a client that respects it is correct for every kind of buffer. What the subcontracting rules forbid is a child adding a requirement the client can’t see. Here the requirement was in the parent’s contract all along, and the child only answers it for its own case.

The catch is that the parent has to be designed for it. Someone has to anticipate that a descendant might run out of room, or go back and add has_room when the first such descendant shows up. That’s the general lesson: when a child class can’t honour its parent’s contract, the fix belongs in the parent’s contract, not in a clever override.

What a child class may do

So far we’ve looked at what a child class must not do. The subcontracting rules also say what it may do: accept more calls, promise more on each call, and guarantee more about its state. An editor buffer with undo needs all three.

Undoable_Buffer remembers the text and cursor before each edit, as a Snapshot. It keeps them on a stack, with the most recent snapshot at index 0, and caps the history at history_limit edits so that memory use stays bounded:

class Snapshot
create
  make(t: String, c: Integer)
  do
    text := t
    cursor := c
  end
feature
  text: String
  cursor: Integer
end

class Undoable_Buffer
inherit Text_Buffer

create
  make_with_limit(n: Integer)
  require
    positive: n > 0
  do
    history_limit := n
  end

feature -- Access
  history_limit: Integer

  can_undo: Boolean
  do
    result := undo_stack.length > 0
  end

  undo_count: Integer
  do
    result := undo_stack.length
  end

feature -- Editing
  -- insert and delete_back are redefined below

  undo
    note "Restore the text and cursor to what they were before the last edit."
  require
    something_to_undo: can_undo
  do
    let previous := undo_stack.get(0)
    undo_stack.remove(0)
    set_cursor(length)
    if length > 0 then
      super.delete_back(length)
    end
    if previous.text.length > 0 then
      super.insert(previous.text)
    end
    set_cursor(previous.cursor)
  ensure
    text_restored: content = old undo_stack.get(0).text
    cursor_restored: cursor = old undo_stack.get(0).cursor
  end

feature -- Implementation
  undo_stack: Array[Snapshot]

  record_edit
  do
    if undo_count = history_limit then
      undo_stack.remove(undo_count - 1)  -- forget the oldest edit
    end
    undo_stack.add_at(0, create Snapshot.make(content, cursor))
  end

invariant
  history_bounded: undo_count <= history_limit
end

Notice how undo rebuilds the text with super.delete_back and super.insert instead of assigning to content. Nex lets only the class that declares a field assign it, so even a child class has to work through Text_Buffer’s routines and their contracts. It calls the super versions so that restoring a snapshot doesn’t itself get recorded as an edit.

Accepting more: a weaker precondition

Text_Buffer.insert rejects an empty string. For an editor that’s an inconvenience: pasting an empty clipboard is a reasonable thing for a user to do. It shouldn’t be a bug, and it shouldn’t leave an empty step in the undo history either. Undoable_Buffer accepts it:

  insert(s: String)
    note "As in Text_Buffer, but an empty string is accepted and ignored."
  require
    nothing_to_insert: s.length = 0
  do
    if s.length > 0 then
      record_edit
      super.insert(s)
    end
  ensure
    undoable: s.length > 0 implies can_undo
    ignored: s.length = 0 implies content = old content
  end

A redefinition’s require is OR-ed with the one it inherits, so the precondition of Undoable_Buffer.insert is effectively (not_empty and room_available) or nothing_to_insert. Every call the parent accepted is still accepted, plus one more kind. A client that knows it has an Undoable_Buffer can rely on the extra case. A client written against Text_Buffer still reads not_empty in the contract it sees, so it shouldn’t count on it, even though the call would go through at runtime.

The OR also means a child can’t sneak in a stronger precondition. Suppose Undoable_Buffer.delete_back declared require small: n <= 2 to keep undo steps small. The combined precondition would be (positive and enough_text_before_cursor) or small, and delete_back(4) would still be accepted. A require in a redefinition can only add to the set of calls the routine accepts.

There’s a second catch: the inherited postconditions still apply to the calls the redefinition now accepts. For an empty string they hold trivially. The length grows by zero and the cursor advances by zero. Compare that with a tempting weakening of delete_back that accepts any positive n and clamps it to the cursor:

  delete_back(n: Integer)
  require
    any_amount: n > 0
  do
    record_edit
    super.delete_back(n.min(cursor))
  end

Calling delete_back(5) on a buffer holding "hi" now fails with Postcondition violation: shrunk. The parent promised that the length shrinks by exactly n, and a clamped delete can’t deliver that. Weakening a precondition only works when the routine can still keep the old promises for the new calls.

Promising more: stronger postconditions

The ensure clauses of the redefined insert don’t replace the parent’s grown and cursor_advanced. They are AND-ed with them, so Undoable_Buffer.insert promises everything Text_Buffer.insert did, plus two things about the history. s.length > 0 implies can_undo reads the way you’d say it: if something was inserted, it can be undone. When s is empty, the clause holds without can_undo being evaluated.

delete_back keeps the parent’s precondition and only adds a promise:

  delete_back(n: Integer)
  do
    record_edit
    super.delete_back(n)
  ensure
    undoable: can_undo
  end

A client written against Text_Buffer still gets shrunk and cursor_moved_back, and never notices the extra one. An editor that knows it has an Undoable_Buffer can enable its Undo menu item right after a Backspace without checking anything. The undo routine is new, so its contract is a first declaration, and any child of Undoable_Buffer will inherit it.

Guaranteeing more: a new invariant

Undoable_Buffer inherits cursor_in_range from Text_Buffer and adds history_bounded: undo_count <= history_limit. Both are checked before and after every call a client makes. If record_edit forgot to drop the oldest snapshot, the first edit after the history filled up would fail with Class invariant violation: history_bounded, and the error would name the routine that left the object in that state.

Putting it all together:

let buf := create Undoable_Buffer.make_with_limit(3)
buf.insert("hello")
buf.insert(", world")
buf.delete_back(7)
assert buf.content = "hello"
buf.undo
assert buf.content = "hello, world"
buf.undo
assert buf.content = "hello"
buf.insert("")  -- accepted, and not recorded
assert buf.undo_count = 1
buf.insert("!")
buf.insert("!")
buf.insert("!")
assert buf.undo_count = 3  -- the oldest edit was forgotten

Adding redo is a good exercise. It needs a second stack, a can_redo query, a redo_cleared: not can_redo postcondition on every edit, and an invariant that bounds both stacks together.

None of these additions was free to make. Each one had to fit around the contract Text_Buffer already published, and Nex checked that it did.

entry.title: Handling command-line arguments in Nex
entry.summary: A Nex program reads its arguments from the predeclared program object. Here is how to get at them, parse them into usable formats, and deal with invalid input gracefully.
entry.content:
Every Nex program starts with two objects already declared: console, for reading and writing text, and program, which describes the running program. program.arguments returns the command-line arguments as an Array[String].

let args: Array[String] := program.arguments

console.print_line("got " + args.length + " argument(s)")
across args as a do
  console.print_line("  " + a)
end

Updated 22 October 2026: this post now uses the predeclared program and console, which arrive in the release after 0.6.2. On 0.6.2 itself, declare them yourself: (create Process).command_line() returns the same arguments, and create Console makes a console.

Save that as args.nex and run it with a few arguments:

$ nex args.nex report.txt "two words" --top 3
got 4 argument(s)
  report.txt
  two words
  --top
  3

Three things to notice:

  • The array holds only your arguments. It starts after the file name, so there is no argv[0] to skip, and with no arguments it is empty.
  • The shell has already split the words. "two words" arrives as one element.
  • Everything is a String. 3 is text until you call to_integer on it.

Reserved runtime flags

nex takes a few options of its own, such as --interpret, --skip-contracts and --classpath. It removes them from the command line wherever they appear, so your program never sees them:

$ nex args.nex one --interpret two --skip-contracts three
got 3 argument(s)
  one
  two
  three

As those names are taken by the runtime, you cannot reuse them as your own options.

A small tool

Here is a complete program that greets someone, with an optional repeat count and an option to shout.

-- greet: say hello from the command line.
--
--   nex greet.nex <name> [--times n] [--shout]

class Options
feature
  name: String
  times: Integer
  shout: Boolean
create
  make(a_name: String, a_times: Integer, a_shout: Boolean)
  require
    has_name: a_name.length > 0
    positive_times: a_times > 0
  do
    name := a_name
    times := a_times
    shout := a_shout
  end
invariant
  has_name: name.length > 0
  positive_times: times > 0
end

function fail(message: String) do
  console.error("greet: " + message)
  console.error("usage: nex greet.nex <name> [--times n] [--shout]")
  exit(2)
end

function to_count(text: String): Integer
do
  result := text.to_integer()
  if result <= 0 then
    fail("--times must be at least 1, got " + text)
  end
rescue
  fail("--times needs a whole number, got " + text)
end

function parse(args: Array[String]): Options
do
  let name: String := ""
  let times: Integer := 1
  let shout: Boolean := false
  let i: Integer := 0
  from
    i := 0
  until
    i = args.length
  do
    let arg: String := args.get(i)
    if arg = "--shout" then
      shout := true
    elseif arg = "--times" then
      if i + 1 = args.length then
        fail("--times needs a value")
      end
      i := i + 1
      times := to_count(args.get(i))
    elseif arg.starts_with("--") then
      fail("unknown option " + arg)
    elseif name = "" then
      name := arg
    else
      fail("unexpected argument " + arg)
    end
    i := i + 1
  end
  if name = "" then
    fail("missing <name>")
  end
  result := create Options.make(name, times, shout)
end

function main() do
  let opts: Options := parse(program.arguments)
  let greeting: String := "Hello, " + opts.name + "!"
  if opts.shout then
    greeting := greeting.to_upper()
  end
  let n: Integer := 0
  from
    n := 0
  until
    n = opts.times
  do
    console.print_line(greeting)
    n := n + 1
  end
end

main()

It behaves the way you would expect a command-line tool to behave:

$ nex greet.nex Ada
Hello, Ada!

$ nex greet.nex Ada --times 3 --shout
HELLO, ADA!
HELLO, ADA!
HELLO, ADA!

$ nex greet.nex Ada --times zero
greet: --times needs a whole number, got zero
usage: nex greet.nex <name> [--times n] [--shout]

$ nex greet.nex Ada --loud
greet: unknown option --loud
usage: nex greet.nex <name> [--times n] [--shout]

The program is short, but there are some patterns worth copying.

Parse once, at the edge

main does not pass the raw array around. It calls parse once and from then on works with an Options object. No other part of the program looks at strings, checks whether an index is in range, or wonders whether times was converted yet.

Bad input is not a bug

Someone typing --times zero has made a mistake, but the program is fine. So parse handles it with ordinary code: it prints a message that names the problem, prints the usage line, and stops. to_integer() raises a Conversion_Error on text that is not a number, and the rescue clause in to_count turns that into the same kind of message.

Errors go to console.error, which writes to standard error, so they stay out of the way when the output is piped somewhere. exit(2) sets the exit status. By convention 0 means success and 2 means the command was used wrongly, which lets a shell script tell the two apart.

A broken parser is a bug

The contracts on Options do a different job. They are not there to check the user. They state what the rest of the program may assume: there is a name, and times is positive. main relies on that when it loops opts.times times without checking anything.

That makes the constructor a checkpoint for the parser itself. Suppose a later edit drops the result <= 0 test from to_count. Nothing about the type of times changes, and the program still compiles. But the first run with a bad value stops at the boundary:

$ nex greet.nex Ada --times 0
Error: Precondition violation: positive_times
  The call at line 70, in parse does not meet the precondition `positive_times` of Options.make.
  called from line 74, in main
  called from line 90

The message names the clause and blames the caller, parse, which is where the missing check belongs. A user should never see this message. If one does, it is telling you about a hole in your validation, not about their typing.

File arguments and relative paths

One thing will surprise you the first time you take a file name as an argument. The nex launcher starts your program from its own installation directory, so a relative path like report.txt does not resolve against the directory you ran the command in. The launcher records that directory, and program.working_directory gives it back to you, so you can resolve the path yourself:

function resolve(raw: String): String
do
  if raw.starts_with("/") then
    result := raw
  else
    result := program.working_directory + "/" + raw
  end
end

The same code is right for the next section too: a compiled program does not go through the launcher, and there working_directory is simply the directory the program runs in.

Shipping it as a jar

nex compile jvm turns the program into a standalone jar. The arguments reach it the same way, so nothing in the code changes:

$ nex compile jvm greet.nex
$ java -jar greet.jar Grace --times 2
Hello, Grace!
Hello, Grace!

Where to go next

  • program can also read the environment (env, has_env) and end the program with a status (exit), and Process starts child processes. The full list is in the system classes reference.
  • If require, ensure and invariant are new to you, the tour of Nex introduces them in a few minutes.
